quests.instruction: You stop a busy colleague with a polite request. Choose the most natural spoken form of the opening “could I ask”.
options: “coud … I ask”: “could” closes with a stop and “I” starts fresh
“cou-ai ask”: the /d/ disappears so the two vowels touch
“cou-dai ask”: the /d/ of “could” is heard at the start of “I”
quests.correctAnswer: “cou-dai ask”: the /d/ of “could” is heard at the start of “I”
quests.hint: Say it softly and quickly, as you would to someone at a desk. Notice what happens between the first two words.
quests.explanation: “Could” ends in /d/ and “I” starts with a vowel sound, so the /d/ usually attaches to “I”: “cou-dai”. Polite requests are often said quickly, so this small shift is common at the start of questions. Knowing it helps you hear “could I” as two familiar words rather than one strange chunk.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /d/ is commonly heard as the beginning of a following vowel-initial word, so “could I” often sounds like “cou-dai”.

quests.instruction: Why does the offer “need a hand” sound like “nee-da hand”?
options: The /d/ closing “need” meets a vowel and is heard as the start of “a”
The weak word “a” is dropped, so the /d/ ends up touching “hand”
Speakers pause briefly after “need” so the /d/ can be released fully before “a”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ closing “need” meets a vowel and is heard as the start of “a”
quests.hint: Say the phrase at the pace of a quick offer to a colleague. Listen for which sound begins the beat that contains “a”.
quests.explanation: The /d/ that finishes “need” is followed by the weak vowel of “a”, so it is heard on that vowel: “nee-da hand”. The word “a” is still there; it just sounds like the end of a linked syllable. This makes offers of help easier to catch when they are said in a rush.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking does not depend on stress: the consonant re-attaches to the following vowel whether that vowel is stressed or weak.

quests.instruction: Choose the version of “wait a second” that fits a quick spoken request.
options: “wait … a second”, with a stop after the /t/ before “a”
“way-ta second”, with the /t/ starting the syllable of “a”
“way-a second”, with the /t/ omitted before the vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “way-ta second”, with the /t/ starting the syllable of “a”
quests.hint: Focus on the two sounds that meet after “way”. Which one starts the next beat when you speed up?
quests.explanation: The /t/ that closes “wait” attaches to the weak vowel of “a”, giving “way-ta second”. Because “a” is so short, it is easy to lose in fast speech. Noticing the link helps you catch it.
quests.phoneticRule: A short unstressed article beginning with a vowel commonly receives the preceding consonant, so the article seems to merge into the previous word.

quests.instruction: Say “in April” at normal speed. What is happening at the boundary between the two words?
options: The two words are separated by a small pause so that “April” starts clearly
The /n/ of “in” is heard at the start of “April”: “i-napril”
The /n/ is left out, so only “i” and “April” remain
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ of “in” is heard at the start of “April”: “i-napril”
quests.hint: Try it inside “My birthday is in April.” Notice which word seems to start with an /n/.
quests.explanation: “In” ends with the nasal consonant /n/, and “April” begins with a vowel, so the /n/ is heard at the start of the second word: “i-napril”. Nasals link smoothly because the voice keeps running. Recognising this helps you hear month names after “in” without searching for an extra word.
quests.phoneticRule: Nasal consonants such as /n/ link to a following vowel like other consonants, and their continuous voicing makes the join smooth.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that best fits how “from a” sounds inside “from a friend”.
options: The /m/ is left out because “a” is too short to take a consonant
“From” and “a” are separated by a pause so the /m/ can be released clearly
The /m/ ending “from” is heard at the start of “a”: “fruh-ma friend”
quests.correctAnswer: The /m/ ending “from” is heard at the start of “a”: “fruh-ma friend”
quests.hint: Say “from a friend” quickly and count the beats. Notice what the closed lips of the /m/ lead into.
quests.explanation: The /m/ that closes “from” meets the weak vowel of “a”, so you hear “fruh-ma friend”. Nasal sounds are voiced, so the join is often easy to hear. Small words such as “from” and “a” are quiet in speech, which is why spotting the link helps you find them.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /m/ links to a following vowel like other nasals, and prepositions such as “from” often appear in this environment.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “on a Sunday”. Which spoken chunking sounds right?
options: “o-na Sunday”, with the /n/ moving onto “a”
“on … a Sunday”, with a stop after “on”
“o-ma Sunday”, with the /n/ changing into an /m/ before “a”
quests.correctAnswer: “o-na Sunday”, with the /n/ moving onto “a”
quests.hint: The word “on” ends in a nasal and “a” is almost a bare vowel. Think about what the nasal does at speed.
quests.explanation: The /n/ at the end of “on” attaches to “a”, giving “o-na Sunday”. The /n/ stays an /n/ and does not change into another nasal. It is a very common way of giving days and times, so you will hear this shape in plans and invitations.
quests.phoneticRule: The same pattern works with any nasal followed by a vowel, so the listening strategy carries over from /n/ to /m/ without change.

quests.instruction: Before you listen, predict: which sound is heard at the start of “us” in “call us”?
options: The /l/ from the end of “call”
The /k/ from the start of “call”
A brief /w/ that connects the two vowels
quests.correctAnswer: The /l/ from the end of “call”
quests.hint: Think about the last sound of “call” and the first sound of “us”. When the words are said without a stop, the mouth is already in position for one of them.
quests.explanation: The /l/ at the end of “call” attaches to “us”, giving “caw-lus”. Because /l/ is a smooth, continuous sound, the join can be so gentle that “us” seems to begin with a soft /l/. Predicting this makes short requests such as “call us” easier to catch.
quests.phoneticRule: In many accents, word-final /l/ is ‘dark’ before a pause but sounds lighter when it links to a following vowel.

quests.instruction: At a petrol station you hear “Fill it up.” Which explanation matches the chunking “fi-li-tup”?
options: “It” is reduced so far that only the /l/ and /p/ remain audible
The /l/ of “fill” is dropped and “it” starts the second beat cleanly
The /l/ of “fill” attaches to “it”, and the /t/ of “it” attaches to “up”
quests.correctAnswer: The /l/ of “fill” attaches to “it”, and the /t/ of “it” attaches to “up”
quests.hint: Tap out the beats in a fast “Fill it up”. Look at which consonants start the second and third beats.
quests.explanation: Both boundaries fit the same rule: a word-final consonant followed by a vowel. The /l/ from “fill” and the /t/ from “it” each start a new beat, giving “fi-li-tup”. That is why the phrase is three quick beats for three words.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking is checked boundary by boundary: /l/ + vowel and /t/ + vowel are separate environments that can occur in the same short chunk.

quests.instruction: Apply the /l/ pattern to “feel awful”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “feel … awful”, with the /l/ held back before a stop
“fee-awful”, with the /l/ dropped before the vowel
“fee-lawful”, with the /l/ starting “awful”
quests.correctAnswer: “fee-lawful”, with the /l/ starting “awful”
quests.hint: Say the phrase as if you are telling a friend how you slept. Notice what sits between the two vowels.
quests.explanation: “Feel” ends in /l/ and “awful” starts with a vowel, so the /l/ moves across: “fee-lawful”. The result is one smooth chunk that carries the feeling. Similar shapes appear in “tell it”, “call in” and “all of”.
quests.phoneticRule: When a word-final /l/ meets a vowel, listeners hear a single syllable boundary just before the vowel, so the vowel-initial word seems to start with /l/.

quests.instruction: Two children are arguing in the next room and you hear “Stop it!” Choose the spoken form that fits.
options: “stop … it”, with the /p/ closing the first word before a stop of air
“sto-pit”, with the /p/ heard at the start of “it”
“sto-it”, with the /p/ left out because “it” already begins with a vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “sto-pit”, with the /p/ heard at the start of “it”
quests.hint: Imagine it shouted from another room. Ask which word gets the burst of air that ends the /p/.
quests.explanation: A plosive such as /p/ is released into the vowel that follows it. In “stop it”, that vowel belongs to “it”, so the /p/ is heard at its start: “sto-pit”. Short commands are said quickly, so the link is worth recognising.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final plosive is commonly released into a following vowel, which makes it sound like the first consonant of the next word.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “job interview” said at conversational speed.
options: The /b/ of “job” is heard at the start of “interview”, so the second word seems to begin with a /b/
“Job” loses its /b/ so that “interview” can start cleanly
The /b/ is weakened into a /p/ before the vowel, so it sounds like “jo-pinterview”
quests.correctAnswer: The /b/ of “job” is heard at the start of “interview”, so the second word seems to begin with a /b/
quests.hint: Say the phrase as if you are checking in at reception. Notice what your lips do just before “interview” starts.
quests.explanation: “Job” ends in /b/ and “interview” starts with a vowel, so the /b/ moves onto it: “jo-binterview”. The consonant keeps its voiced quality, so it does not turn into /p/. Long words that begin with a vowel are easy to mishear unless you expect this link.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiced plosives such as /b/ keep their voicing when they link to a following vowel; linking changes the syllable boundary, not the identity of the consonant.

quests.instruction: Apply the same idea: which spoken form fits “wake up” in “Time to wake up!”?
options: “way-up”, with the /k/ removed so the vowels join
“way-kup”, with the /k/ starting “up”
“wake … up”, with a stop of air after the /k/
quests.correctAnswer: “way-kup”, with the /k/ starting “up”
quests.hint: Think of an alarm-clock reminder said fast. The /k/ ends the first word; where does its release land?
quests.explanation: The /k/ at the end of “wake” is released into “up”, giving “way-kup”. Phrasal verbs with “up”, “on”, “off” and “out” are very common, so this shape will appear often.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiceless plosives (/p t k/) link with a following vowel in the same way as /b d g/; only the voicing quality differs.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form is the most natural version of “give up” in “Don’t give up!”?
options: “give … up”, with the /v/ held before a stop
“gi-up”, with the /v/ left out
“gi-vup”, with the /v/ starting “up”
quests.correctAnswer: “gi-vup”, with the /v/ starting “up”
quests.hint: Say it as encouragement, with energy and speed. Notice which sound is still buzzing when “up” begins.
quests.explanation: The /v/ that ends “give” is voiced and continuous, so it flows straight into “up”: “gi-vup”. Because the buzz carries on, the link can be easier to hear than after a stop like /p/. It is a useful chunk in everyday encouragement.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiced fricatives such as /v/ keep their voicing when they link to a following vowel, so the join is heard as a buzz at the start of the next word.

quests.instruction: In “brush it off”, which two sounds are heard at the start of “it” and “off”?
options: /b/ from “brush”, then /ʃ/
/ʃ/ from “brush”, then /t/ from “it”
/ʃ/ from “brush”, then /f/ from “off”
quests.correctAnswer: /ʃ/ from “brush”, then /t/ from “it”
quests.hint: Say the phrase at the speed of a friend’s quick advice, and listen for the sounds that end the first two words.
quests.explanation: The “sh” sound ending “brush” links to “it”, and the /t/ ending “it” links to “off”: “bru-shi-toff”. Each word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a vowel, so both boundaries follow the same pattern. You will hear a similar chain in short pieces of advice like this one.
quests.phoneticRule: The fricative /ʃ/ links to a following vowel, and the same chunk can contain a second link from the following stop.

quests.instruction: Use the pattern for “laugh at me”. Which chunking is right?
options: “la-fat me”, with the /f/ starting “at”
“laugh … at me”, with a stop after the /f/
“la-vat me”, with the /f/ voiced into a /v/
quests.correctAnswer: “la-fat me”, with the /f/ starting “at”
quests.hint: Say “Don’t laugh at me” quickly. Listen for a soft, airy sound just before “at”.
quests.explanation: “Laugh” ends with /f/, and “at” starts with a vowel, so the /f/ starts the next syllable: “la-fat me”. The /f/ stays voiceless, so it does not become /v/. There is no link before “me”, because “at” ends in a consonant and “me” begins with one.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking does not change the voicing of a fricative: /f/ stays voiceless and /v/ stays voiced.

quests.instruction: Which consonant is heard at the start of “out” in a quick “find out”?
options: The /d/ that ends “find”
The /n/ that comes just before the /d/
Both /n/ and /d/ move together onto “out”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ that ends “find”
quests.hint: Say “Did you find out?” and listen for the last sound of “find” and what it touches.
quests.explanation: “Find” ends in the cluster /nd/. When “out” follows, the /d/ is heard at its start: “fine-dout”. The /n/ stays with the first word because /nd/ is not a normal way for English words to begin. Knowing which part travels helps you predict the break.
quests.phoneticRule: In a final cluster such as /nd/ that cannot begin an English word, only the last consonant re-attaches to a following vowel.

quests.instruction: Compare “first aid” with “find out”. Which description fits “first aid”?
options: The /t/ is dropped, because clusters are simplified when a word ends in /st/
The /t/ is kept; it is heard at the start of “aid”, often together with the /s/: “fur-staid”
The /s/ is dropped and only the /t/ starts “aid”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ is kept; it is heard at the start of “aid”, often together with the /s/: “fur-staid”
quests.hint: Ask yourself which consonant sequences can begin an English word, then check whether “st” is one of them.
quests.explanation: “St” is a normal way to begin English words (stop, start), so both sounds can move onto “aid”: “fur-staid”. Some speakers shift only the /t/. Either way the /t/ is heard, because a vowel follows; dropping it is more typical before a consonant, which you will study later.
quests.phoneticRule: Clusters that can begin English words, such as /st/, /sk/ and /sp/, may re-attach as a whole to a following vowel-initial word, while other clusters release only their final consonant.

quests.instruction: Apply both ideas to “just in time”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “jus … in time”, with a stop after the /t/
“ju-in time”, with the whole cluster dropped
“ju-stin time”, with /st/ starting “in”
quests.correctAnswer: “ju-stin time”, with /st/ starting “in”
quests.hint: The first word ends in /st/, the same cluster as before. Say “just in time” quickly and note where the hissing sound falls.
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/ and “in” starts with a vowel, so the cluster can shift onto “in”: “ju-stin time”. You can hear the same shape in “first aid”. Listening for a vowel after a final cluster helps you avoid mishearing “stin” as part of a new word.
quests.phoneticRule: A cluster's ability to re-attach depends on whether it forms a possible word beginning; /st/ does, so “just in” can be heard as “ju-stin”.

quests.instruction: Someone says “Good night” at the door. Does the linking pattern from earlier levels apply between the words?
options: Yes: the /d/ of “good” attaches to “night” to form “goo-dnight”
Yes: the /t/ at the end of “night” attaches back to “good”
No: “night” begins with a consonant, so there is no vowel for the /d/ to attach to
quests.correctAnswer: No: “night” begins with a consonant, so there is no vowel for the /d/ to attach to
quests.hint: Check what kind of sound begins the second word. The earlier pattern needs one particular kind of sound there.
quests.explanation: Consonant-to-vowel linking needs a vowel sound after the final consonant. “Night” begins with /n/, so “good night” is a consonant-to-consonant boundary: the /d/ ends its word and the /n/ begins the next. Other changes are possible in fast speech, but they are a different topic from this link.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant-to-vowel linking requires a vowel sound after the word-final consonant; a consonant + consonant boundary is not linked in this sense.

quests.instruction: In “book a table”, how many boundaries have a consonant-to-vowel link?
options: One: the /k/ of “book” attaches to “a”; “a table” has no such link
Two: both “book a” and “a table” link
None: “book” ends in a stop, and stops cannot link
quests.correctAnswer: One: the /k/ of “book” attaches to “a”; “a table” has no such link
quests.hint: For each boundary, check the last sound of the first word and the first sound of the second. Which boundary has a consonant followed by a vowel?
quests.explanation: Only the first boundary fits: “book” ends in /k/ and “a” is a vowel, giving “boo-ka”. Between “a” and “table”, a vowel meets the consonant /t/, so there is nothing to link. Checking each boundary separately keeps you from expecting a link everywhere.
quests.phoneticRule: Each word boundary must be checked separately: only consonant + vowel boundaries show consonant-to-vowel linking.

quests.instruction: You hear “Same time next week?” Which comment about the boundary in “next week” is accurate?
options: It is a consonant + consonant boundary, so the earlier linking pattern does not apply
The /t/ moves onto “week” to give “nek-stweek”
“Week” starts with a vowel sound in fast speech, which lets the /t/ link
quests.correctAnswer: It is a consonant + consonant boundary, so the earlier linking pattern does not apply
quests.hint: Think about how the first sound of “week” is made. Do your lips and tongue block or narrow the airflow?
quests.explanation: “Week” begins with /w/, a consonant sound, even though it behaves a little like a vowel. So the words meet consonant to consonant, and the earlier linking pattern does not apply. Later levels show what does happen at boundaries like this one.
quests.phoneticRule: The glides /w/ and /j/ count as consonants for consonant-to-vowel linking, so a word beginning with either of them does not receive a linked consonant.

quests.instruction: Choose the description that fits “have a shower” said as part of a morning routine.
options: Each word starts with its own clean beginning: “have / a / shower”
The /v/ of “have” is heard at the start of “a”: “ha-va shower”
The weak “a” attaches to “shower”: “have ashower”
quests.correctAnswer: The /v/ of “have” is heard at the start of “a”: “ha-va shower”
quests.hint: Start with the last sound of “have”. Then decide which word the tiny vowel that follows is closer to.
quests.explanation: “Have” ends in /v/ and “a” is a weak vowel, so the /v/ links to it: “ha-va shower”. The small word “a” therefore sounds like the end of “ha-va”, not the beginning of “shower”. This helps you hear routine phrases as three words even at speed.
quests.phoneticRule: The link forms an onset for the weak vowel of the article, so the article is heard as the second half of the linked syllable rather than as part of the following noun.

quests.instruction: Which explanation fits the way “get up at seven” is chunked in fast speech?
options: Only the first boundary links; “up at” stays separate because “at” is a small word
The /t/ and /p/ are both removed, so “get”, “up” and “at” slide together as vowels
The /t/ of “get” attaches to “up”, and the /p/ of “up” attaches to “at”: “ge-tu-pat seven”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “get” attaches to “up”, and the /p/ of “up” attaches to “at”: “ge-tu-pat seven”
quests.hint: Underline each word that ends in a consonant and is followed by a vowel-initial word. Then say the phrase and see if your underlines match the joins you hear.
quests.explanation: Two boundaries qualify: /t/ + “up” and /p/ + “at”. Both consonants start the next beat, giving “ge-tu-pat seven”. Time phrases such as this are common in daily-routine talk, and “pat” can sound like a separate word if you do not expect the link.
quests.phoneticRule: In a phrase with several short vowel-initial words, each qualifying boundary links independently, producing a chain of shifted syllable edges.

quests.instruction: Choose the spoken form of “work out at eight” you would expect in a quick chat about your week.
options: “work … out … at eight”, with a small stop before each vowel-initial word
“wur-kou-tat eight”, with /k/ and /t/ each starting the next beat
“wur-ou-at eight”, with the /k/ and /t/ dropped so the vowels touch
quests.correctAnswer: “wur-kou-tat eight”, with /k/ and /t/ each starting the next beat
quests.hint: Mark two consonant-to-vowel boundaries in the phrase and check where each consonant lands.
quests.explanation: The /k/ that ends “work” joins “out”, and the /t/ that ends “out” joins “at”: “wur-kou-tat eight”. The logic is the same as in earlier levels, applied across four words. Practising with routines helps you recognise the pattern when people talk about their day.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant-to-vowel linking extends to longer chunks without changing its logic; only the number of qualifying boundaries increases.

quests.instruction: Predict how the start of “Will it rain later?” will sound. Which chunking is most likely?
options: “wi-lit rain”, with the /l/ starting “it”
“will … it rain”, with a break before “it”
“wi-it rain”, with the /l/ dropped so the vowels join
quests.correctAnswer: “wi-lit rain”, with the /l/ starting “it”
quests.hint: Predict first, then say it the way you would ask a friend about the weather. Notice which word the /l/ seems to join.
quests.explanation: The /l/ at the end of “will” attaches to “it”, so the opening of the question sounds like “wi-lit rain”. Question openers with “will”, “would” or “can” are short and quick, so the shifted edges are easy to miss. Predicting them trains you to hear the whole question.
quests.phoneticRule: Because auxiliaries and pronouns sit side by side at the start of a question, the auxiliary's final consonant often shifts onto the pronoun, so the question stem is heard as one quick chunk.

quests.instruction: Choose the best explanation for how “have I” sounds at the start of “Have I told you?”
options: The /v/ is dropped and “have” becomes “ha”, so two vowels meet
The /v/ stays with “have”, and “I” gets a short break before it
The /v/ is heard at the start of “I”, giving “ha-vai”
quests.correctAnswer: The /v/ is heard at the start of “I”, giving “ha-vai”
quests.hint: Say the first two words alone, quickly, as if they were one word. Which consonant do you think begins the second syllable?
quests.explanation: “Have” ends in /v/, and “I” is a vowel sound, so the /v/ moves across: “ha-vai”. “Have I” can then sound like a single word, which is why some learners cannot pick out the pronoun. Listening for the link helps you separate the two.
quests.phoneticRule: The pronoun “I” starts with a vowel sound, so it readily receives the final consonant of a preceding auxiliary, as in “have I”, “did I” and “can I”.

quests.instruction: A teacher asks the room, “Can anyone help?” Which chunking fits the words “can anyone help”?
options: “can … anyone help”, with a break before “anyone”
“kuh-nen-ee-wun help”, with the /n/ starting “anyone”
“kuh-ee-wun help”, with the /n/ dropped after the weak vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “kuh-nen-ee-wun help”, with the /n/ starting “anyone”
quests.hint: Say it as if you are calling out to a room of people. Where does the /n/ sit relative to the word “anyone”?
quests.explanation: The weak word “can” ends in /n/, and “anyone” starts with a vowel, so the /n/ moves onto it: “kuh-nen-ee-wun help”. Group questions often start this way, so the shape is worth recognising. The word “can” is also weak here, which is a topic for a later stage.
quests.phoneticRule: Questions beginning with “can” followed by a vowel-initial subject show the same n-linking pattern as other auxiliary + pronoun sequences.

quests.instruction: Which pair of words in “It’s an old photo” is NOT linked by a consonant-to-vowel connection?
options: “old photo”
“It’s an”
“an old”
quests.correctAnswer: “old photo”
quests.hint: Test each pair: does the first word end in a consonant sound, and does the second start with a vowel sound? One pair fails the test.
quests.explanation: “It’s an” links /s/ to “an” (“it-san”), and “an old” links /n/ to “old” (“a-nold”). “Old photo” is /d/ + /f/, consonant to consonant, so no such link happens. Sorting boundaries like this is what makes fast speech feel less mysterious.
quests.phoneticRule: A boundary shows consonant-to-vowel linking only when the first word ends in a consonant sound and the second begins with a vowel sound; both conditions must hold.

quests.instruction: Your teacher says “Hand it in on Monday.” Which version matches fluent speech?
options: “hand … it … in … on Monday”, each word clearly separated
“han-di-ti-non Monday”, with three consonants shifting forward
“han-dit in on Monday”, with only the /d/ moving forward
quests.correctAnswer: “han-di-ti-non Monday”, with three consonants shifting forward
quests.hint: Find every place where a word-final consonant meets a vowel-initial word, and mark them all before you choose.
quests.explanation: Three boundaries qualify: /d/ + “it”, /t/ + “in”, and /n/ + “on”. Each consonant starts the next syllable, so the words form one smooth chain before “Monday”. A long chain like this is easier to decode when you read it boundary by boundary.
quests.phoneticRule: Long chunks are decoded by working through boundaries in order: every consonant + vowel boundary contributes a shifted syllable edge, and consonant + consonant boundaries do not.

quests.instruction: At a hotel you hear “Check in at the desk.” Which statement is accurate?
options: Every boundary in the phrase links because the words are said quickly
Only the boundary between “in” and “at” links, since “check in” is a single verb
“Check in” and “in at” link, but “at the” and “the desk” do not
quests.correctAnswer: “Check in” and “in at” link, but “at the” and “the desk” do not
quests.hint: Go boundary by boundary and ask whether a consonant meets a vowel. Ignore how quickly the phrase is said.
quests.explanation: “Check” ends in /k/ and “in” starts with a vowel, so you hear “che-kin”. “In” ends in /n/ and “at” starts with a vowel, so you hear “i-nat”. “At the” is consonant-to-consonant and “the desk” is vowel-to-consonant, so neither shows this link. Speed does not create links where the sounds do not allow them.
quests.phoneticRule: Speed does not create links: a link needs a consonant + vowel boundary, and boundaries without that combination are unaffected by this pattern.
